accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE Mathematics programmes of study KS3 (2013) statistics strand: construct and interpret tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (or bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data; describe distributions of discrete, continuous and grouped data. Class intervals use inequality notation 150 ≤ h < 160. The adult text flags that touching bars with equal widths are a frequency diagram at KS3 and that true histograms plot frequency density at GCSE Higher (AQA 8300 specification), so the lab's histogram label is qualified.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the classic slips: any number is numerical (shirt number prediction and the mean test, tag catnum), rounded age or time is discrete (step 3 prediction and challenge, tag round), shoe size is continuous (sorted as discrete with the 5.3 test), grouped heights drawn with gaps (chart picker rejects bar chart with gaps for grouped heights, tag gaps), a line graph for categories (tag line), and confusing labels with amounts (tag label).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdtype combines a names-or-numbers card sort, a zoomable number line that splits 152 to 153 cm three times while a siblings line shows nothing between 2 and 3, a discrete versus continuous sort, a chart picker that draws each chart type on four data sets with suits or does not suit feedback, and a two-branch data classification tree. No other flagship lab classifies data types; the shingle gate passed against all flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds the in-between test by zooming into heights themselves and seeing 152.55 cm then 152.5555 cm appear while siblings stay at 2 or 3. The chart picker shows why a pie chart fails for grouped heights and why gaps mislead, before the done message names the rule: gaps for categories and counts, touching bars for grouped measurements, a line for readings over time.

predictions.evidence: Two or more locked predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: Numerical, it is a number for shirt numbers; No, nothing in between for a height between 152.5 and 152.6 cm; Discrete, it goes 11, 12, 13 for age. Each prediction is echoed back in the done message with the reason it was right or wrong.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge asks about puzzle times recorded to the nearest second and offers Discrete, because it is rounded as the tempting distractor. Each wrong answer gets a tagged message explaining the error (rounding, label versus amount, gaps), and wrong card drops in the sorts explain the mean test or the counted versus measured test rather than just saying no.

readability.evidence: Validator readability gates pass for the learner audience: kid paragraphs use short sentences and one term at a time (variable, categorical, discrete, continuous) with concrete examples like eye colour, siblings and 152.55 cm; adult paragraphs were rewritten into shorter sentences to land under the FK grade 9.5 target while keeping KS3 terms.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases; every paragraph carries a definition, test, example or named mistake. Practice and mastery explanations show the working, e.g. {=10*k} ÷ 10 = {k} classes and counting 0 to {n} gives {=n+1} lines in the siblings vertical line chart.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: every Show me reached the tick within 3.4 seconds, tree nodes were repositioned and widened so Continuous fits on a 390 px screen, chart picker buttons and sort cards are full tap targets, and the zoom works by tap or drag on the number line.

accessibility.evidence: Axe passed in light and dark themes; the canvas has an aria-label and every state change is announced in the live feedback text; tiles use an opaque base under the green or red tint so labels keep contrast; every task can be done with buttons, not only drags.
